cases.title: Two weeks in a hotel gym and worried about his squat
cases.situation: Luis, 39, lifting 5 years, strength, nothing hurts. Squat 275 × 5, bench 205 × 5. He has two weeks of work travel. The hotel gym has dumbbells up to 50 lb, one adjustable bench and a cable machine. He types: "What do I do so I don't lose my squat?"
cases.short: Train 2 to 3 times a week there with hard split squats on the 50s. First barbell squat back at 260 × 5, then 275 again if it moves well.
cases.today: Travel: the coach rebuilds those days for the equipment he has, keeps the main movement patterns, and goes back to the normal plan when he returns. Coming back: the app takes 10% off after 1 to 2 weeks away, but it counts days since his last logged workout. If he logs the hotel sessions, it takes nothing off and plans 275 on day one. The rules don't say what replaces a heavy squat or what to do about a lift he hasn't touched.
cases.rec: Two or three sessions a week on the trip. Squat stand-in: Bulgarian split squat with the 50s, 3 sets of 8 to 12 each leg at effort 8 to 9 out of 10, plus goblet squat with the 50 lowered for 3 seconds. Keep a hinge (dumbbell Romanian deadlift), a press and a cable row. Back home, no blanket 10% drop, since he trained. Only the lift he didn't do with a bar starts lighter: squat 260 × 5 (about 5% down) for the first session, back to 275 next time if it lands at the target effort. If he trains fewer than once a week on the trip, today's 10% rule applies as written.
cases.why: Spiering's 2021 review found strength holds for up to 32 weeks on one session a week if the weight stays heavy, and the detraining guide cites a pooled analysis of 103 studies where max strength barely moved in the first 4 weeks of no training at all. So two weeks is low risk. The catch: 50s are not heavy for him, and Liao's review found single-leg training builds two-leg strength a little less well than two-leg training. That gap is why I start the bar 5% light; the 5% itself is my judgment. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Maintaining physical performance: the minimal dose of exercise needed to preserve endurance and strength over time (Spiering, Mujika, Sharp, Foulis, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2021; abstract read)
A Guide to Detraining: What to Expect, How to Mitigate Losses, and How to Get Back to Full Strength (Greg Nuckols, Stronger by Science, 2022)

Effects of unilateral vs. bilateral resistance training interventions on measures of strength, jump, linear and change of direction speed: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Liao, Nassis, Bishop, Yang, Bian, Li, Biology of Sport, 2022)

cases.reply: You won't lose it in two weeks. Train 2 or 3 times: Bulgarian split squats with the 50s, 3 sets of 8 to 12 each leg, hard, plus slow goblet squats, dumbbell RDLs, a press and a cable row. First squat day back is 260 × 5, and if that moves well you're at 275 again the session after.

cases.title: Missed the bottom of the range twice, both after 5 hours of sleep
cases.situation: Nate, 27, lifting 3 years, nothing hurts. Bench 185 for sets of 5, range 3 to 6. Two sessions in a row his last set was 2 reps. Both were morning sessions after about 5 hours of sleep, with a yellow check-in. He types: "I slept badly both days. Don't drop my weight."
cases.short: Reset anyway to 175 and say why. Short sleep explains a small part of it, not a last set of 2.
cases.today: Any set under the bottom of the range counts as a miss. One miss keeps the weight. Two in a row resets it, 5% for him: 185 becomes 175. The app checks this before it looks at sleep or energy, so a yellow day changes nothing here (yellow only takes a set off). A red day stops increases but does not stop a reset.
cases.rec: Same as today: reset to 175 and build back. Tell him plainly that the bad nights probably cost him a little and the reset costs him two to three weeks. If short sleep is normal for his mornings, the weight has to fit the days he really trains. What would change the call: if either miss came on a red day (under 5 hours, or unwell), I would not count that one, and I would hold 185 for one more try. That part is new and is my judgment.
cases.why: Craven's 2022 analysis: sleep loss took about 3% off strength on average, morning sessions were mostly unaffected, and cutting sleep short (as opposed to none at all) had no clear effect. 3% of 185 is about 5 lb, which is the size of the reset. So 175 is a target he can hit on a bad night too, which fits how the head coach sets targets. The studies varied a lot and most were on men. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review (Craven, McCartney, Desbrow, Sabapathy, Bellinger, Roberts, Irwin, Sports Medicine, 2022)

cases.reply: I'm taking bench to 175 next session. The short nights probably cost you a rep, but a last set of 2 twice in a row says 185 is right at your limit for now. Hit 6s at 175 and you'll be back at 185 in two to three weeks.

cases.title: Five weeks of skipped lunges: "I feel stupid doing them"
cases.areaName: an athlete who avoids a lift
cases.situation: Priya, 44, lifting 2 years, general strength, full gym, nothing hurts. For 5 weeks she has skipped or swapped every lunge and split squat. She types: "My balance is awful, I feel stupid doing them."
cases.short: Respect it and swap to leg press or squats. Offer a hand-on-the-rack version once, as her choice, then drop it.
cases.today: Anything she dislikes is swapped for an equivalent. After a lift has been swapped away again and again, the app asks once whether to stop suggesting it. Nothing says whether the coach should offer an easier version first, and step-ups are not in the exercise list.
cases.rec: Swap to leg press or squats and keep her training. When the app asks its question, the coach offers one easier option, once and with no pressure: reverse lunges or split squats with a hand on the rack, 2 sets of 8 each leg. If she says no, stop suggesting single-leg work and don't raise it again unless she does. Her legs lose nothing she needs for general strength. What would change the call: a goal that needs one-leg strength (a sport, hiking with a pack), or she asks for balance work herself.
cases.why: Liao's review: two-leg training built two-leg strength slightly better than one-leg training, and one-leg strength came out about the same either way. Adams's 2023 review of 66 trials in people aged about 40 to 60 found ordinary strength training improved balance by itself, and no trial in that age group measured falls at all. So I found no evidence that she needs lunges. The studies were small and many were weak. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Effects of unilateral vs. bilateral resistance training interventions on measures of strength, jump, linear and change of direction speed: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Liao, Nassis, Bishop, Yang, Bian, Li, Biology of Sport, 2022)
Effects of Physical Activity Interventions on Strength, Balance and Falls in Middle-Aged Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Adams and others, Sports Medicine - Open, 2023)

cases.reply: No problem, lunges are out. I've put leg press in their place, and your squats cover the rest. If you ever want to try them holding the rack for balance, say so and I'll add 2 easy sets. Otherwise I won't bring them up again.

cases.title: "Free weights scare me. Can it all be machines?"
cases.situation: Dana, 26, first week, wants general fitness, full commercial gym, nothing hurts. She types: "Free weights scare me. Can my whole program be machines?"
cases.short: Yes. Build it all on machines and cables now, and offer one free-weight lift once after 4 to 6 weeks.
cases.today: Variations fit her equipment and preferences. If she unticks the free weights in her equipment list and rebuilds, the app can fill squat (leg press, Smith or hack squat, leg extension), push (chest press, shoulder press, fly), pull (lat pulldown, cable row, face pull), arms and calves from machines and cables. One gap: the only machine for the back of the legs and hips is the leg curl; there is no machine hip-hinge lift in the list. Machine lifts are all treated as accessories, so she gets 8 to 15 reps. Nothing says whether the coach brings free weights up later.
cases.rec: Yes, all machines, no argument. Start at 10 to 15 reps with enough weight that the last reps feel like real work (effort 6 to 8 out of 10). For the hip gap use leg curl plus glute bridges on the floor. After 4 to 6 weeks, offer one free-weight lift once, with a reason she cares about: a goblet squat or dumbbell Romanian deadlift, light, 2 sets. If she says no, leave it and ask again only at the start of a new block or if she raises it. What would change the call: a goal that names a barbell lift.
cases.why: The 2023 analysis of 13 studies and 1,016 people found no difference between machines and free weights for strength on neutral tests, muscle size or jumping. Strength showed up best on whatever people trained with. The college of sports medicine's position stand tells novices to include both kinds, so machines-only is a slight step away from it, on preference. Strong evidence.

sources.t: Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2023; abstract read, authors not shown on the page)
Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults (American College of Sports Medicine position stand, 2009; read on a university-hosted copy)

cases.reply: Yes, it can all be machines, and you'll get just as strong and fit that way. Untick the free weights in your equipment list and tap Rebuild program, and I'll set it up at 10 to 15 reps per set. In a month or so I'll offer you one dumbbell lift to try. It's your call then too.

cases.title: "I take every set to failure. Stop telling me not to."
cases.situation: Vince, 35, lifting 9 years, wants size, 5 days a week, full gym, nothing hurts. He types: "I take every set to failure, always have. Stop telling me to leave reps in the tank."
cases.short: Failure is fine on machines, cables, isolation lifts and last sets. On heavy barbell squats, deadlifts and unspotted bench, stop 1 to 2 reps short. Say it once.
cases.today: Main lifts for size are 6 to 10 reps at effort 7 to 9 out of 10, and a lift earns more weight only when every set reaches the top at or under the target effort. Lighter weeks: nothing to failure. The rules don't say where failure is allowed or what to do when an athlete insists.
cases.rec: For an experienced lifter chasing size: failure is fine on machines, cables and isolation lifts, and on the last set of dumbbell work. On barbell squats, deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts and bench without a spotter or safety bars, the coach recommends stopping 1 to 2 reps short (effort 8 to 9). It says this once and stops repeating it. If he still wants failure on a barbell lift, the coach asks for safety bars or a spotter and lets him. Lighter weeks stay failure-free. If his reps fall off sharply from set to set or his check-ins turn red, the coach cuts a set instead of arguing. Beginners stay at today's efforts.
cases.why: He has a point for size. The 2022 analysis found no overall difference between failure and stopping short, with a small size edge for failure in trained lifters. Refalo found going to true failure no better than stopping just short. Robinson's 2024 analysis found size gains rise the closer sets get to failure while strength is the same across a wide range. None of them measured injuries; where failure is unsafe is coaching judgment. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: A systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of Sport and Health Science, 2022; abstract read on the journal index, authors not shown)
Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis (Refalo, Helms, Trexler, Hamilton, Fyfe, Sports Medicine, 2023)

Exploring the dose-response relationship between estimated resistance training proximity to failure, strength gain, and muscle hypertrophy: a series of meta-regressions (Robinson, Pelland, Remmert, Refalo, Jukic, Steele, Zourdos, Sports Medicine, 2024; abstract read)

cases.reply: Fair. Go to failure on machines, cables, isolation work and your last dumbbell sets, and I'll stop mentioning it. On heavy barbell squats, deadlifts and bench with no spotter, I'd still stop 1 or 2 reps short. If you want to go all the way there, set the safety bars first.

cases.title: Creatine: loading week, and "is it bad for your kidneys?"
cases.situation: Sean, 41, lifting 1 year, wants muscle, healthy, takes no medication. He types: "Should I take creatine? Do I need a loading week? I read it's bad for your kidneys."
cases.short: 3 to 5 g a day, no loading week needed. Fine for healthy kidneys. Kidney problems or kidney-related medication: ask his doctor first.
cases.today: Creatine at 3 to 5 g a day is fine to mention, with no brands. The rules don't cover loading, the kidney question, or who should check with a doctor first.
cases.rec: Same dose as today, with three additions. Loading: not needed; 3 to 5 g every day gets to the same place, just more slowly, and the coach never suggests the big loading doses. Kidneys: in healthy adults the research has not found harm at this dose. Ask a doctor first, and the coach gives no dose, when the athlete mentions kidney disease or past kidney trouble, one kidney, diabetes, high blood pressure, medication that affects the kidneys, or heavy regular use of ibuprofen-type painkillers. One practical line: tell the doctor before a blood test, because creatine can shift a routine kidney reading. It stays optional; the coach never pushes it.
cases.why: The sports nutrition society's 2017 position stand calls creatine safe and well tolerated in healthy people, short and long term. Its 2021 follow-up paper gives 3 to 5 g a day as the well-tolerated dose. Cleveland Clinic says loading is not necessary and brings more stomach upset. Scripps Health lists who should ask a doctor first and explains the blood-test point. Only the abstracts of the two papers would open; the loading and doctor-first details come from the two hospital pages. Strong evidence.

sources.t: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine (Kreider and others, Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2017; abstract read)

Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show? (Antonio and others, Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2021; abstract read)
Is the Creatine Loading Phase Worth Doing? (Cleveland Clinic, 2024)
Is Creatine Safe for Your Kidneys? (Scripps Health, 2026)

cases.reply: Creatine is worth it if you want it: 3 to 5 g a day, every day, and no loading week needed. In healthy adults the research hasn't found kidney harm at that dose. If you've ever had kidney trouble or take medication that affects your kidneys, check with your doctor first. And mention it before any blood test, since it can shift one of the kidney readings.

cases.title: Cold plunge right after every lifting session
cases.situation: Tess, 34, lifting 4 years, wants muscle, full gym, nothing hurts. Her gym has a cold plunge and a sauna. She does a 10-minute cold plunge right after every lifting session. She types: "Is that helping my recovery?"
cases.short: For a muscle goal, move the plunge off lifting days or well away from the session. Sauna after lifting is fine. Her choice in the end.
cases.rec: For an athlete whose goal is muscle: tell her once that cold water straight after lifting may blunt the growth she is training for, and suggest moving it to rest days or a separate time of day. No study pins down how many hours apart is enough, so the coach gives no number. Cold right after is fine when feeling fresh matters more than growth: a tournament, back-to-back hard days, or a goal that isn't size. Sauna after lifting is fine: drink water, and get out if she feels dizzy. If she keeps the plunge anyway, that's her call and the coach drops it.
cases.why: A 12-week trial (Roberts, 2015) had people sit in cold water for 10 minutes after each session, her exact habit; strength and muscle rose more in the group that did easy cycling instead. Piñero's 2024 review of 8 studies found lifting alone likely builds more muscle than lifting plus cold water, but rated the studies fair to poor. For sauna I found one 6-week trial (10 minutes of infrared sauna after training): no extra growth and no harm. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Cold water immersion after strength training, 12-week trial by Roberts and others (The Journal of Physiology, 2015; abstract read, title not shown on the page as read)
University of Queensland news release on the same trial, 10 August 2015 (page title not shown as read)

Throwing cold water on muscle growth: a systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of post-exercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy (Piñero and others, European Journal of Sport Science, 2024; abstract read)
Effects of repeated use of post-exercise infrared sauna on neuromuscular performance and muscle hypertrophy (Ahokas, Hanstock, Kyröläinen, Ihalainen, Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 2025)

cases.reply: It may feel good, but right after lifting it's probably costing you some of the muscle you're training for. Move the plunge to rest days or a different time of day, and use the sauna after lifting if you want something. If the plunge is the part you love, keep it. Just know the trade.

cases.title: Back squat from the front: knees drift in on the last three reps
cases.situation: Kim, 29, lifting 18 months, general strength, full gym, nothing hurts. Back squat, 185 × 6, filmed from the front. Reps 1 to 3: knees track over the toes. Reps 4 to 6: both knees drift inward about 2 to 3 inches as she drives out of the bottom, the right more than the left, and her hips shift slightly to the right. Depth is fine and the bar stays level.
cases.short: Knees caving as she tires is the main fault. Cue "push the floor apart", drop to 165 and build back.
cases.today: From the front the app scores depth, control on the way down and whether the reps look alike. Bar path and back angle are not judged from this angle. It does measure how wide the knees are next to the ankles and whether the bar tilts, but neither counts in the score, and the knee measure is taken at the very bottom, while hers cave on the way up. It doesn't measure a hip shift; the coach only sees that in the frames. There is no fault list yet.
cases.rec:
Fault: Knees caving in on the way up in reps 4 to 6 is the main one. The hip shift to the right comes second and likely goes with it.
Cue: "Push the floor apart and keep your knees over your little toes as you stand."
Severity: Moderate. It only shows when she is tired and nothing hurts. Major if it shows from rep 1, gets bigger, or the knee starts to hurt (then the pain rules apply as they do today).
Lower the weight: Yes, about 10% next session (185 to 165), then build back with normal jumps. Form breaking on the late reps means the weight went up too fast.
If it keeps happening: Paused squats in the warm-up (2 sets of 5, 2-second pause at the bottom, knees held out), split squats and hip thrusts for the hips, and film from the front again in two weeks. If the right side still leads, add a calf and ankle stretch for that side.
cases.why: Sources disagree on how serious this is. University physical therapy teaching slides link it to knee injuries and name weak hip muscles and stiff ankles as causes, with cues like "drive your knees out". A lifting site reports a 2024 study that found no difference in injury rates and argues a small cave is not dangerous; I read only that report, not the study. A lab study found that limiting ankle bend made the knees move inward more. Sources also split on squatting with a band round the knees, so I left it out. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: Common Faults with Barbell Back Squat: Implications for Injury & How to Address Them (Brooks and Humphrey, University of North Carolina physical therapy program slides, about 2024)
Article on whether knees caving during squats is bad (Phil Blechman, BarBend, updated 2025; title taken from the link)

Effect of Limiting Ankle-Dorsiflexion Range of Motion on Lower Extremity Kinematics and Muscle-Activation Patterns During a Squat (Macrum, Bell, Boling, Lewek, Padua, Journal of Sport Rehabilitation, 2012)

cases.reply: Kim, reps 1 to 3 look good. On 4 to 6 your knees drift in as you stand up, the right more than the left. Take it to 165 next session and think "push the floor apart" on the way up. Film the front again in two weeks so I can check it.

cases.title: First filmed set: heels lift, and he wants 45 lb
cases.situation: Greg, 48, started 3 weeks ago, general fitness, full gym, nothing hurts. His first filmed set: goblet squat, 35 lb × 10, side-on. On every rep his heels lift about half an inch at the bottom, his torso tips well forward, the dumbbell drifts away from his chest, and he stops about 3 inches above parallel. Reps 8 to 10 get faster and shallower. He logs the effort as 5 to 6 out of 10 and asks to go to 45 lb next time. He has tight calves from a desk job and old ankle sprains that don't hurt now.
cases.today: Side-on, the app marks the set down for depth (no rep reaches parallel), for the hands drifting forward, and it may mark the quick last reps as dropped. It checks the torso only for change from rep to rep, so a lean that is the same every rep costs nothing, and it doesn't measure heels at all; the coach only sees those in the frames. There is no fault list yet. On weight: a beginner's lift goes up about 5% when every set hits the top of the range at or under the target effort, never more than 10% in one step. On the numbers he has earned progress, which at this weight means a rep added to every set first and then 40. 45 is a 29% jump, which the app refuses. Form faults don't hold the weight back today.
cases.rec:
Fault: Heels lifting is the main one. The forward tip, the dumbbell drifting out and the short depth all follow from it.
Cue: "Whole foot down, weight tight to your chest, sit down between your heels." Setup: heels on a small wedge or two flat plates, about an inch.
Severity: Moderate. It is a learning fault at a light weight and nothing hurts. Minor once the heels stay down. Major only if something starts to hurt (then the pain rules apply as they do today).
Lower the weight: No, and no to 45 for now. Stay at 35 with the heels raised, 3 seconds down, 12 to 15 reps. Done to full depth, 35 will stop feeling easy. When 3 sets of 12 are full depth with heels down, go to 40, then 45. Give him the harder work he wants on leg press, where form isn't in question.
If it keeps happening: Squat to a box set at the depth where his heels stay down and lower the box over time. Add a calf stretch and an ankle drill to the warm-up. Film side-on again in two weeks.
cases.why: The trainer guide I read says the weight in front should let a beginner sit taller and deeper, gives 10 to 15 controlled reps as the starting point, and says to add load only when it is controlled cleanly. Physical therapy teaching slides call a heel raise a quick fix for stiff ankles. A lab study found limiting ankle bend cut squat depth by about 15 degrees of knee bend. No trial tests holding the weight while form is learned; that part follows the head coach's earlier answers. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: The Goblet Squat: A Trainer's Coaching and Programming Guide (Heather Cherry, NASM, 2022, updated 2026)
Common Faults with Barbell Back Squat: Implications for Injury & How to Address Them (Brooks and Humphrey, University of North Carolina physical therapy program slides, about 2024)

Effect of Limiting Ankle-Dorsiflexion Range of Motion on Lower Extremity Kinematics and Muscle-Activation Patterns During a Squat (Macrum, Bell, Boling, Lewek, Padua, Journal of Sport Rehabilitation, 2012)

cases.reply: Good first video, Greg. Not 45 yet: your heels come up on every rep, and that's what tips you forward and cuts the depth. Next time keep 35, put your heels on two flat plates, hug the weight to your chest and take 3 seconds down for 12 to 15 reps. When 3 sets look like that, we go to 40, then 45.

data.said: 35 feels easy now. Can I go up to 45 next time?
data.checkin: Slept 7 h · Energy 78 · Soreness: mild (legs) · Stress: low · Green
log: RPE 4, legs very sore, light day
RPE 5 to 6, full plan, set 2 filmed
data.food: Not tracking food yet; logs weight once a week.
data.follow: Earlier call (reviewed Nov 25): in his first week Greg was so sore he could barely do stairs. The coach kept him training, with leg work at half the sets for two weeks. Soreness is now mild, he hasn't missed a session, and he is back on the full plan and proud of it.

cases.title: Stuck at 70 lb of help: "Am I ever getting one?"
cases.situation: Tasha, 37, lifting 7 months, 175 lb, general strength, full gym, nothing hurts, wants her first pull-up. Her gym has an assisted pull-up machine. In three weeks she went from 90 lb of help to 70, aiming for 3 × 6. Her last three sessions at 70 lb of help were all 6, 5, 4 reps, with the last set as hard as she can go. Lat pulldown is up to 85 × 10. She types: "I've stalled. Am I ever getting one?"
cases.today: The plateau guide says under 3 weeks flat is normal noise and to say so, then check logging, recovery, food and form before changing the training, one change at a time for 3 to 4 weeks. From the earlier call: use the assisted machine, test one pull-up every 4 weeks, pull-ups back in the plan at 3 clean ones. The assisted machine and slow lowers are not in the app's exercise list, so the app can't track or progress them; the coach describes them in words. Nothing says how to step the help down.
cases.rec: Tell her she hasn't stalled: three sessions is a week and a half, and her pulldown rose over the same weeks. The step from 80 to 70 was simply too big. One change now: keep 70 lb of help but do 5 sets of 3, each set stopped with a rep in hand, twice a week. Build to 5 sets of 5, then go to 60 and repeat. If the machine moves in 5 lb steps, use those. Keep lat pulldown progressing as it is. Only if she is flat for 3 to 4 more weeks, make the second change: 2 to 3 slow lowers of 3 to 5 seconds before the machine sets. Test one real pull-up every 4 weeks, fresh, at the start of a session. On timing, be honest: likely months, not weeks, and no promised date. Never mention her weight or shape; the help number is the only measure she needs.
cases.why: Sources agree on the tools and disagree on the order. A hospital sports medicine guide puts the assisted machine first and says to cut the help gradually. The Marine Corps guide prefers slow lowers of 3 to 7 seconds and many easy sets spread out, and discourages assist machines. A coach's pull-up series limits slow lowers to three days a week because they are hard to recover from. None gives a timeline or tests one method against another, so the timing and the 5 sets of 3 are my judgment. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: How to get your first pull-up (Harrison Ross, Parkview Sports Medicine, 2024)
Pull-up Training Guide (U.S. Marine Corps)
Beginner Pull-Up Series: Negatives and Increasing the Loading (Justin Lind, Breaking Muscle, 2017, updated 2021)

cases.reply: I think you will, and you haven't stalled: your pulldown went from 80 to 85 × 10 in the same three weeks. The jump from 80 lb of help to 70 was a big one, so next session stay at 70 but do 5 sets of 3, stopping each set with a rep left. When that's 5 sets of 5 we go to 60, and we'll try a real one every 4 weeks. Expect months, not weeks.

data.said: I've stalled. Am I ever getting one?
data.checkin: Slept 6 h · Energy 58 · Soreness: none · Stress: high (work) · Yellow
data.food: Logs most days, close to maintenance at about 2,100 kcal; protein about 115 g against a 140 g target.
data.follow: Earlier call (reviewed Nov 25): the coach asked whether her gym has an assisted pull-up machine, which was the head coach's call: use it if there is one. It does. For three weeks she has done 3 sets on it, starting at 90 lb of help and reaching 70. It worked at first and then stuck: her last three sessions at 70 were 6, 5, 4 reps each time.

program.heading: Week 1 of 4, as Kedge built it
program.athlete: Sam, 29. Lifting 2 years, wants strength and size, full gym, 4 days a week, about 60 minutes, nothing hurts. Squat 245 × 5, bench 185 × 5, deadlift 295 × 5.
days: Back squat 4 × 5 at effort 7–8; Romanian deadlift 3 × 8; walking lunge 3 × 10 each leg; leg curl 3 × 12; plank 3 × 40 s
Bench press 4 × 5; barbell row 4 × 8; overhead press 3 × 8; lat pulldown 3 × 10; curl 2 × 12
Deadlift 3 × 5; front squat 3 × 6; Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8; leg press 2 × 12; calf raise 3 × 12
Overhead press 4 × 5; weighted pull-up 4 × 6; incline dumbbell press 3 × 10; cable row 3 × 10; lateral raise 3 × 15; triceps pushdown 2 × 12
program.note: Weeks 2 and 3 add weight when every set reaches the top at the target effort. Week 4 is a lighter week.
